$comment: Generated from the spec model with the schemas and examples. Drives the plugin prompt table, widget_examples and the app renderer registry test.

types.summary: Labelled numbers: one renders as a hero, two to six as a row or grid, up to six small ones in a strip.
limits: 1–6 items. Labels ≤ 40 characters; notes ≤ 120.
Sparklines: 2–60 points.
Values must be numbers (or times for countdown); use `display` only when formatting can’t express it.
types.fallback: One line per item: `<label>: <value><unit> (<delta> <period>)`. Example: “Sales: $1,284 so far today (+12% vs last Tuesday).”
use: One to six key numbers with deltas: daily revenue, installs, steps vs goal.
A countdown to a time: boarding, a deadline, an auction end.
A strip of small facts: last night’s sleep, HRV and resting heart rate.
avoid: A single number inside a sentence: write it in the prose.
A series over time worth reading: use `chart` (a sparkline in `metric` is decoration, not data).
Progress toward a target where the gap matters: use `meter`.
More than six numbers: use `table`.

types.cue: a value against a target or range
types.summary: A value within a range or against a target: one bar, a bar per item, nested rings, or an arc with zones.
limits: bar: 0–8 items (one renders as a hero); ring: 1–3; arc: exactly 1.
Every item needs `max` or `target`: a number without a scale is a `metric`.
Labels ≤ 40 characters, notes ≤ 120, headline ≤ 60, widget note ≤ 200; ≤ 5 zones.
Values are numbers or null. Percentages are fractions (0.91 with `format: percent` and `max: 1`).
types.fallback: One line per item: `<label>: <value> of <target> (<percent>), <zone or what’s left>`, then the headline and note. Example: “October budget: $1,840 of $2,000 spent (92%, nearly spent). $160 left with 12 days to go.” An unknown value is written “unknown” with the reason, never 0.
use: A budget, quota or cap: $1,840 of $2,000 spent in October, API calls this month, ad spend against its limit.
Goals for the day as nested rings: steps, active minutes and stand hours; treadmill minutes and steps.
A score inside named zones on an arc: readiness 82 (Good) from sleep and recovery.
Several values against their own targets, one bar each: protein, fibre and sugar for the day; disks on Studio Mac.

Test coverage against the project’s target: the `coverage` parser (lcov, Cobertura, coverage.py, Go) fills one item per metric (lines, branches) with `format: percent` and `max: 1`; the target comes from the tool call.
avoid: A number with no target or range: use `metric`.
How a value moved over time, even against a goal: use `chart` with a `target` rule.
More than 8 values, or values someone will want to sort: use `table`.
A pass / fail judgement with reasons (is it safe, which is better): use `verdict`.
Progress through the stages of a job (3 of 5 done): use `steps`. Coverage that meets its target with nothing to act on deserves one sentence, not a widget.

types.cue: a series over time, a breakdown
types.summary: A series over time, a few bars to compare, or the parts of a whole, in ink and greys, with the number that matters said in words.
limits: ≤ 3 series, each with exactly as many values as `x.values`.
line and area: 2–120 points; bar and stacked: 2–14 bars (group days by week beyond two weeks); share: 2–4 parts.
One baseline, one target, one callout. Labels ≤ 40 characters, callout ≤ 24, note ≤ 280.
Values are numbers or null: never strings, never 0 for missing.
types.fallback: The headline, the shape in one sentence, the key values, then the note. Example: “Resting heart rate: 61 bpm today, above your usual range (52–58) for the last 3 days after two weeks inside it. That often follows short sleep or a stressful stretch; an early night may help. It’s an observation, not a diagnosis.” For share, one line per part with its value and percentage.
use: A health or fitness trend against the person’s own baseline: resting heart rate for 14 days, sleep, weight, with a note that observes and suggests a gentle next step.
Daily or weekly counts with the one that matters called out: installs this week, revenue per day, commits.
Up to three series compared: this year vs last, iOS vs Android, planned vs actual (stacked when they add up).
A breakdown of a whole: spending by category, storage by kind, traffic by source (`kind: share`).
Numbers that already sit in a file: the `csv` parser (also `tsv`, `jsonl`) fills `x` and up to three `series` from the columns the call names.
avoid: One to six current numbers: use `metric` (its sparkline is decoration, not data).
A value against a target right now: use `meter`.
Exact values someone will read or sort: use `table`.
Days with marks (habits, streaks, activity per day): use `calendar`.
More than three series, or a pie: split the question, or use `table`. Never a pie on a phone.

types.summary: Days with marks: a habit’s weeks with a streak, a month with dated dots, or activity per day as intensity.
limits: weeks: 1–12 weeks; month: one month. ≤ 400 marks: one per day for check and intensity, ≤ 3 per day for dot.
Dot labels ≤ 24 characters, at most four different labels (the legend fits one line); notes ≤ 80.
`level` is 0–1; `streak.current` and `streak.best` are whole numbers.
types.fallback: The streak, then one line per week or the list of marked days. Example: “Knee exercises: 16-day streak (best 21). Missed 23 and 27 September; every day since 28 September done; today 1 of 2 sessions.” Month: “October: dentist Oct 8, 10:30 AM; electricity bill due Oct 20 ($64); tax return deadline Oct 21.” Intensity: the busiest and quietest days with their counts.
use: A habit or plan with a streak: knee exercises twice a day, medication taken, a language lesson, a daily walk.
A month with dated things: plans, bills due, deadlines, school holidays.
Activity per day as intensity: commits, workouts, words written, energy used at home.
Rehab or training adherence over several weeks, with today’s partial progress.
avoid: A schedule with times and places: use `agenda` (the `ics` parser fills it).
Daily numbers whose exact values matter: use `chart` (bars) or `table`.
Today’s to-dos: use `checklist`.
A single streak number with no days to show: use `metric`.

types.cue: a decision or a safety check
types.summary: A judgement with its reasons: a pick between options, an is-it-safe check, or a scorecard, with every criterion and how it is known.
limits: 1–12 criteria. Labels and values ≤ 40 characters, notes ≤ 120; outcome label ≤ 60, reason ≤ 200, would_change ≤ 200.
`outcome.state: ok` (and the envelope `state: ok`) is invalid with any criterion `unverified` or `critical`.
score: `outcome.score` and a `score` on every criterion. safety: one criterion per declared item and no `confidence`; critical when any is critical, else unverified when any is unverified.
types.fallback: The outcome first, then every criterion with its value and how it is known, then what would change it. Example: “Not verified: don’t serve the chicken satay bowl to Maya until someone checks the sauce and dressing. Peanuts: no data for “satay sauce”. Tree nuts: not present (ingredient list on the menu). Sesame: no data for “house dressing”.” Never shorten a safety fallback to the outcome alone.
use: Allergen and diet checks: a dish against everyone’s declared allergens, one criterion per allergen, with where each answer came from.
A recommendation after research: the database for an app, the flight to book, the laptop to buy, with confidence and what would change the pick.
A scorecard: an App Store listing, a pull request against the team’s checklist, a flat against the person’s must-haves.
Compatibility checks: does this charger work with the laptop, does the plugin support the gateway’s version.
avoid: Options side by side for the person to weigh: use `compare` (weights re-rank on the device).
The status of systems or jobs: use `status`. A CI run where everything passed: one sentence, no widget.
A single number against a target: use `meter`.
An opinion with nothing checkable behind it: write it in prose (“I think…”).

types.cue: sides with scores: match, poll, A/B
types.summary: Two to four sides with scores and a status: a match, a race, a poll or an A/B test.
limits: 2–4 sides. Names ≤ 60 characters, details ≤ 120, period ≤ 24, note ≤ 120.
At most one winner, only when final; a test needs `significance.reached: true` for one.
Scores are numbers or null (a rate is a fraction with `format: percent`).
types.fallback: Status and period, the sides with their scores, then the details. Example: “Kansas City Chiefs 24–17 Buffalo Bills, live in Q3 8:14 (NFL, Week 7). Mahomes 2 TD passes; Allen 2 TD runs. Halftime 14–10.” A test: “Paywall test (trial starts), finished: new paywall 5.1% of 2,412 visitors vs current 4.2% of 2,388, +0.9 points, significant at 95% confidence.”
use: A live or final score: football with the minute, basketball with the quarter and clock.
An A/B test: the rate per variant, visitors, the change in points, and whether it is significant.
A poll’s standing: votes per option in a group chat, while open and once closed.
A race between up to four: a sales contest, Bots on a benchmark, the top four of a Grand Prix.
avoid: A league table or more than four sides: use `table`.
Options with criteria to weigh: use `compare`, or `verdict` for a pick.
Asking people to vote: use `choice`, then show the standing here.
How a score moved over time: use `chart`.

types.summary: Rows of things, each with a leading visual, a title, a subtitle and a trailing value or tag: plain, ranked, grouped into a digest, or in lanes.
limits: 0–50 rows (an empty list should carry `empty_text`); the client shows the first 5, then Show all.
Titles ≤ 120 characters (two lines), subtitles ≤ 120 (one line); ≤ 2 tags and ≤ 2 actions per row.
≤ 8 groups, ≤ 4 count chips. Lanes: 2–4 groups read well; more scroll sideways.
types.fallback: The title and counts, then one line per row, problems first, under group headings: `<title> — <subtitle>: <value> (was <previous>, <delta>) [tags]`. Example: “Apartments in Brooklyn, tonight: 3 new, 2 price drops, 1 gone. Price drops: 412 5th St, Apt 3R — $1,198,000 (was $1,240,000, −3.4%); 88 Berkeley Pl — $869,000 (was $899,000, −3.3%). New: Prospect Park West, park view — $1,650,000 … Gone: 211 7th Ave (was $975,000).” Ranked: “3. hiking app (▲ 4, was 7)”.
use: A set of similar things to scan: open tickets, posts in the queue, scheduled jobs (failures first).
Ranks and how they moved: keyword positions, a leaderboard, a research shortlist.
A digest of changes since last time, grouped with counts: New 3, Price drops 2, Gone 1.
Stages side by side (`layout: lanes`): a launch board, a sales pipeline.

Linter and analyser findings: the `sarif` parser fills `items` (one per finding, worst first, `subtitle` “file:line · rule”, a severity tag: error → critical, warning → warning, note → info, `url` to the file); `csv` fills rows from a sheet.
avoid: Things the person ticks off: use `checklist`.
Several numbers per row that are worth comparing across rows: use `table`.
Events in time order with times: use `timeline` (or `agenda` for a day).
One thing in depth (a listing, a product): use `entity`; its labelled facts: `details`.
Pull request reviews, a failing run’s jobs: use `steps` for the run, the app’s DiffCard for code.

types.summary: Items the person ticks off, optionally grouped with progress; a tick is a request the agent confirms.
limits: 0–50 items (an empty list should carry `empty_text`); ≤ 12 groups.
Labels ≤ 120 characters, detail ≤ 120; ≤ 2 tags and ≤ 2 actions per item.
The client shows the first two groups (or 8 items), then Show more.
types.fallback: The title and progress, then one line per item with a box: `[x]` or `[ ]`, the label, detail and tags, grouped under headings. Example: “Shopping for the week (4 of 9): Produce — [x] Tomatoes, 2 lb; [x] Spinach, 8 oz; [ ] Lemons, 3; [ ] Cilantro, 1 bunch. Dairy — [x] Greek yogurt, 32 oz; [ ] Feta, 8 oz; [ ] Oat milk, half gallon …” Platforms without widgets let the person reply “got lemons”.
use: A shopping list grouped by aisle, from the week’s meal plan.
Today’s medication, private, with times and “Taken 08:04”.
Overdue and due-soon tasks with who they’re for, late first.
Chores by person or room; a packing list by bag; a release checklist where each ticked item says how it is known (`evidence`).
avoid: Progress through stages the agent runs (setup, a deploy, an order): use `steps`.
Rows to read, not tick: use `list`.
One question with a few answers: use `choice`; several answers to send together: `form`.
A plan with nested parts: use `outline`.
Scheduled reminders with times through the day: use `agenda`.

types.summary: A small grid of values: rows of things by a few columns of numbers, with an optional total, sortable on the device.
limits: 1–6 columns (≤ 4 recommended on iPhone), 0–50 rows.
Column labels ≤ 24 characters; text cells ≤ 120.
The client shows the first 8 rows (2 blocks when reflowed), then Show all.
types.fallback: The title, then one line per row: `<first cell>: <label> <value>, …`, then the total. Example: “Portfolio this week (vs last week): AAPL: 60 shares, $14,820 value (+4%); MSFT: 30 shares, $13,560 (−2%); VOO: 12, $6,720 (no change); NVDA: 70, $13,110 (+6%). Total: 172 shares, $48,210 (+2%).” Never a Markdown table: it doesn’t survive notifications.
use: Per-app numbers with changes: installs, revenue, change vs last week, and a total.
Coverage per file from the `coverage` parser (lcov, Cobertura, coverage.py); any sheet from `csv` / `tsv` / `jsonl` (`columns` picks and orders).
Spending per category against a budget; energy per room; a standings table.
Specs of 2–4 options side by side, when there is no pick to make.
avoid: One to six headline numbers: use `metric`.
A series over time: use `chart`.
Options to choose between with criteria and a pick: use `compare`.
Labelled facts about one thing: use `details`.
More than 6 columns or 50 rows: show the part that matters (a `table` of the top 10, `metric` for the totals) and attach the file; the Inspector opens CSVs.

types.summary: Labelled values about one thing — an invoice, a booking, a machine’s specs — optionally in titled sections, with mono values and local Copy.
limits: 1–6 sections, 1–12 fields each; ≤ 24 fields in all reads well.
Labels ≤ 40 characters; text values ≤ 280; detail ≤ 120.
One `emphasis` per widget.
types.fallback: The title, then one `<label>: <value>` per field, sections as headings. Example: “Invoice INV-0042, sent Oct 1: Amount $2,400.00; Client Bluefin Studio LLC; Due Tue, Oct 20 (in 4 days); Status unpaid; Pay to Chase checking •• 4410.” Masked values stay masked in the fallback.
use: An invoice or receipt: amount, client, due, status, bank details.
A booking: flight, departure, booking code, hotel, check-in.
Specs and status of one thing: a machine, a device, a subscription, a parcel.
The fields of a record the agent found: a support ticket, a company, a contact.
avoid: One thing with a photo, a rating and actions (a listing, a place): use `entity`.
The same fields for several things: use `table`.
Before and after of the same fields: use `diff`.
A boarding pass or ticket to scan: use `pass`.
Passwords, API keys or full card numbers: never in a widget; the app’s secure request handles secrets.

types.summary: A tree up to four levels deep: a plan with progress, a structure, or files with what changed; branches fold.
limits: Depth ≤ 4; ≤ 30 top-level nodes, ≤ 20 children per node, ≤ 60 nodes in all.
Labels ≤ 120 characters; detail ≤ 120.
The client shows the first 12 visible rows, then Show all.
types.fallback: The title and progress, then one line per node, indented two spaces per level, with the state as a word or a mark (`[x]` done, `[~]` running, `[ ]` waiting, `[!]` failed or blocked, `[?]` unknown). Example: “Postgres migration (3 of 8): [x] Move the database; [~] Switch the app over — [x] Point staging at the new host; [~] Run the migration on a copy (running now, 12 of 48 tables); [ ] Swap production; [ ] Clean up.” Files: “Changed files (3): Sources/Sync/Reconnect.swift (modified), Sources/Sync/Backoff.swift (added), Package.swift (modified).”
use: A plan with phases and steps and where it is: a migration, a move, a launch.
Files a change touched, by folder, with A / M / D / R tags and links that open them (mode files).
A structure: the sections of a report, a site map, the parts of a project.
A breakdown the person explores: a budget by area, a course syllabus.
avoid: A flat set of steps in order, live: use `steps`.
Items the person ticks off: use `checklist`.
The code changes themselves: the app’s DiffCard (or `code` for a snippet).
A flat set of things: use `list`; events in time: `timeline`.

types.summary: What changed: fields before and after (a listing’s price, a flight’s time), or a passage of text with removed and added words marked.
limits: Values: 0–20 rows (an empty diff should carry `empty_text`); labels ≤ 40, values ≤ 280 characters.
Text: before and after ≤ 4,000 characters each; send the changed passage, not the whole document.
For code use DiffCard.
types.fallback: Values: the title, then `<label>: <before> → <after> (<delta>)` per row. Example: “412 5th St changed since 10 PM yesterday: Price $1,240,000 → $1,198,000 (−3.4%); Status For sale → Under offer; Viewing not offered → Sat 10 AM–12 PM.” Text: “Suggested edit to README, Sync section. Before: “…” After: “…””.
use: A watched thing that changed: a listing (price, status, viewing), a product’s price, a contract’s terms.
A schedule change: a flight’s departure and gate, a delivery window.
A suggested edit to prose: a README section, an email, a bio (mode text).
Settings before and after a change the agent made (with a `receipt` if it can be undone).
avoid: Code changes: the app’s DiffCard (or `code` for a snippet); never a text diff of code.
Many things that changed a little: use `list` with `previous` and `delta` (a digest).
A change waiting for the person’s OK: use `approval` (with `subject.change`).
A number and how it moved over time: use `metric` or `chart`.

types.summary: Events in order on a rail: a package on its way, a history, an incident log, a day of travel, with the current event ringed.
limits: 0–30 events; 6 show when there are more than 8, the rest behind Show all. At most one `current`.
Title ≤ 80 characters, detail ≤ 120; ≤ 2 actions per event.
`kind: incident` needs a date-time on every event (no day-only or unknown times); an empty `events` needs the envelope’s `empty_text`. Both, and the single `current`, are checked by the schema.
types.fallback: One line per event, in order: `<time> — <title> (<detail>)`, with the state as a word when it isn’t done (“now”, “expected”, “failed”). Example: “Package from Portland, arrives today. Tue — Ordered (wall light, order 4471). Wed — Shipped (UPS 1Z999AA10123456784, from Portland). 9:12 AM — now: in Brooklyn, out for delivery (14 stops before you). Today 1–3 PM — expected: delivered.”
use: Package and order tracking: ordered, shipped, out for delivery, the expected window.
A day of travel (`direction: future`): leave home, the flight, the train, the hotel check-in.
An incident log (`kind: incident`): errors start, someone paged, a rollback, recovered, each with its exact time and who.
A history: an app review’s path through App Review, a ticket’s life, a property’s price changes.
avoid: Progress through fixed stages where the gaps matter more than the times (a CI run, a multi-step task): use `steps`.
A day’s or week’s schedule with spans and free time: use `agenda`.
The incident itself, with impact and the next step: use `alert` (link this timeline from it or stack the two).
A boarding pass or ticket to show at a gate: use `pass`; directions from A to B: use `route`.
A delivered parcel: one sentence, not a widget.

types.summary: A schedule: one day as blocks with free time and the now line, or the days ahead as one line each.
limits: 0–50 events; view days spans 2–14 days. Up to 3 all-day items show, the rest as “+2 all-day”.
Title ≤ 80, note ≤ 80, day notes ≤ 40; ≤ 2 tags and ≤ 2 actions per event; ≤ 12 people (the line names two and “+3”).
Times in RFC 3339 with offsets; dates for all-day items only.
types.fallback: The date, then one line per item in time order: `<start>–<end> <title> (<place>, with <people>; <note>)`, all-day items first, free time as “Free <from>–<to>” when complete, the flag in words. Example: “Friday, October 16. All day: Mom’s birthday. 9–9:30 AM Stand-up (Zoom). Free 9:30–11 AM. 11 AM–12 PM Dentist (200 W 57th St; leave by 10:40). Free 12–2 PM. 2–3:30 PM Paywall review, with Ada and Ops.”
use: Today’s schedule in a morning brief, with the next thing to leave for flagged.
The week ahead (`view: days`): the first event and a count per day, travel days called out.
A day the agent planned or changed (moved a meeting, found an hour), the changed block tagged.

From an .ics file: `from_file` with `parser: ics` fills `events` (DTSTART / DTEND → start / end, DATE values → all_day, SUMMARY → title, LOCATION → place, ATTENDEE CN → people, STATUS and PARTSTAT → state), expanding repeats within the range.
avoid: Events in sequence where the times are history, not a schedule (a parcel, an incident, a travel day as legs): use `timeline`.
Days with marks (habits, streaks, a month of workouts): use `calendar`.
Proposed times for the person to pick: use `choice` with `style: times`.
One event with its details and RSVP: use `entity` (`kind: event`).

types.cue: one thing: listing, place, PR, file
types.summary: One thing — a listing, product, person, place, event, file, link, review or pull request — as a card with its visual, the facts that matter and what to do next.
limits: One thing per widget. Name ≤ 120, eyebrow ≤ 80, detail ≤ 160, note ≤ 120, body ≤ 600.
≤ 8 attributes, ≤ 4 tags, ≤ 12 people (five faces show, then “+7”), ≤ 4 buttons with one primary.
One visual; images ≤ 10 MB when fetched by the gateway.

Each recipe needs its block (checked by the schema): listing and product → `price`; place → `place`; event → `when`; file → `file` and `url`; link → `url`; review → `rating` and `body`; pull_request → `pull_request`. A rating above its `scale` is invalid (checked by the plugin).
types.fallback: The kind and name, then the facts in the order shown, then the link: `<kind>: <name> — <eyebrow>. <price> (was <was>). <attributes>. <tags>. <url>`. Example: “Listing: 412 5th St, Apt 3R — for sale, Park Slope, Brooklyn. $1,198,000 (was $1,240,000, −3.4%). 2 bedrooms, 950 sq ft, balcony, elevator. Price drop; viewing Saturday. StreetEasy, listed 9 days ago: https://listings.example.com/412-5th-st-apt-3r”.
use: Things to buy or rent (`listing`, `product`): a photo on top, the price with what it was, attribute chips (2 bd, 950 sq ft), tags (Price drop), Save / Book a Viewing.
People and places (`person`, `place`): an avatar or map snapshot, the role or distance, reach buttons and Directions drawn from `contact` and `place`.
Things in time and files (`event`, `file`, `link`): a date tile with RSVP, a file that opens in the Inspector, a link with its real domain and a thumbnail.
Work items (`review`, `pull_request`): an App Store review with stars and Draft a Reply; a pull request with checks, reviews, +/− and Merge as a request.
avoid: Several things of the same kind (tonight’s listings, the open pull requests): use `list` (with leading visuals); two to four to choose between: use `compare`.
Many labelled fields (an invoice, a booking’s details): use `details`.
A gallery or a voice note: use `media`.
A boarding pass or ticket to scan: use `pass`; a schedule: use `agenda`.
The health of a service or a CI run: use `status` or `steps`; a green pull request that merged needs one sentence, not a card.

types.cue: images, a gallery, a voice note
types.summary: Images, a video or a voice note in the reply: one item large with its caption, a grid or carousel of up to twelve, or an audio player with a waveform.
limits: 1–12 items; the grid shows four tiles, the carousel all twelve. More than twelve: an `open` action to the full gallery.
alt ≤ 200 (required on every item), caption ≤ 200, credit ≤ 80, transcript ≤ 4,000.
Images and videos ≤ 10 MB each when fetched by the gateway; waveform 16–120 samples.
types.fallback: One line per item: `<caption or alt> (<photo | video, 0:34 | audio, 1:42>)`, then the transcript for audio. Remote links stay out unless the person needs them. Example: “412 5th St, 12 photos: living room with a green sofa; the bedroom; the kitchen; the view from the balcony over 5th Avenue… (12 photos).” For a voice note: “Voice note from Maya (1:42): “Hi, I’m running late…””
use: One image with a caption: today’s lunch special, a screenshot of the bug, a generated image.
Photos of one thing (`layout: grid` or `carousel`): a listing’s rooms, a product from every side.
A voice note or a recording (`kind: audio`) with its waveform, duration and transcript.
A short video with its poster: a screen recording of the fix, a clip from a camera.
avoid: One thing with a photo and facts (price, rooms, rating): use `entity`; the photo is its visual.
A chart drawn as an image: use `chart`, so the numbers are data and VoiceOver can read them.
A file to open or download (a PDF, a ZIP): use `entity` with `kind: file`.
Code or a log as a screenshot: use `code`.

types.summary: A block of code, a log or command output in monospace, with copy, folding, and an optional result of running it.
limits: `text` ≤ 20,000 characters; `lines` 1–200, each ≤ 2,000 characters; the whole payload ≤ 64 KB.
`result.output` ≤ 4,000 characters; `command` ≤ 500.
The client folds after 12 lines (5 for a log in compact density); nothing is truncated silently.
Exactly one of `text` and `lines`.
types.fallback:
The title, the code in a fenced block with its language (the one place Markdown is allowed in fallback_text, so other platforms keep it monospace), then the result on its own line. A log: the counts, then the last lines as `time LEVEL text`, repeats as “(×12)”, and where the full log is. Example: “Backoff for reconnects (Swift, for Sync/Reconnect.swift):
```swift
func backoff(_ n: Int) -> Double {
  min(5, 0.25 * pow(2, Double(n)))
}
```
Ran in 0.4 s: 0.25 0.5 1 2 4 5.”
use: A suggested snippet with what it returned when Hermes ran it: “Ran in 0.4 s · 0.25 0.5 1 2 4 5”.
The tail of a log around a problem: levels, counts, repeats folded. The `log` parser fills it from a file (`lines`, `counts`, `omitted`).
What a failing command or test printed, with its exit code. The `junit` parser puts each failure (test, message, file:line) in `lines` at level error.
A few lines of a gateway file (`path` and `range`), opened in the Inspector with a tap.
avoid: A code diff or Hermes’s own file changes: the app’s diff card and the Changes tab; before and after text is `diff`.
A run that fully passed: one sentence (“All 214 tests passed in 38 s”), no widget.
Pass and fail counts or stages of a pipeline: `steps` (with `code` for the failures) or `metric`.
A whole file or a very long log: point to it with `entity` (file) and open it in the Inspector.
One command or value inside a sentence: inline `code` in the prose.

types.summary: The references behind an answer, numbered to match [1] markers in the prose and tagged with how far to trust them; one source with an excerpt renders as a quote.
limits: 0–20 sources; a reply rarely needs more than 6.
Titles ≤ 160 characters, excerpts ≤ 500, `used_for` ≤ 120, notes ≤ 80.
Quote layout: exactly one source, with an excerpt (in the schema).
Every URL is https:// or hermes-file:.
types.fallback: One line per source, numbered as in the prose: `[n] <title> — <domain or site>, <date> (<trust>): <url>`. A quote: the excerpt in quotation marks, then the attribution and the link. Example: “Sources: [1] EU AI Act: implementing guidelines — eur-lex.europa.eu, 14 Oct 2026 (primary source): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/… [2] What the new AI rules mean for apps — theverge.com, 15 Oct 2026 (secondary): https://www.theverge.com/… [3] Apple to delay AI features in the EU — a post on X, not confirmed (unverified).”
use: The sources behind a research answer or a ranked verdict, numbered to match [1], [2] in the reply.
A news story with “why it matters”, where a rumour must stay tagged unverified next to the confirmed report.
The exact words of a rule, a contract clause or a release note, as a quote with its locator.
An option comparison’s evidence, under a `compare`.
avoid: One link worth opening on its own (an article, a product page): `entity` (link).
A news story told as a story, with “why it matters”: `summary` (story recipe), with `sources` under it.
Evidence for one row of a checklist, verdict or steps: that row’s `evidence` caption.
Search results to pick from: `list` (or `choice` when one is to be picked).

types.summary: The weather for one place: now, the next hours with the chance of rain, the days ahead on a shared range scale, and one plain-language tip.
limits: ≤ 12 hours, ≤ 10 days, ≤ 3 alerts.
Tip ≤ 120 characters; alert titles ≤ 80.
One place per widget: several places are several compact widgets in a `stack`.
Chances are 0–1; temperatures are numbers in `unit` or null.
types.fallback: The place and day, now with the unit, high and low, the hours worth knowing (rain), the days as `Fri 46–54°F, rain 80%`, then the tip and any alert. Example: “New York, Thursday: 58°F and partly cloudy (feels 55°), high 63°, low 48°. Rain from 4 PM (70%), 60% at 6 PM. Take an umbrella for the walk home. (Apple Weather, 10:05 AM)”
use: The morning brief: now, the next hours and a tip (“Rain from 4 PM. Take an umbrella for the walk home.”), compact inside the stack.
The days ahead for planning: a trip, a weekend run, a garden job.
A trip day in an itinerary: compact, one line per destination.
An official warning (wind, storms, heat) as the banner on top.
avoid: “It’s 14° and sunny”: one sentence, no widget.
A weather series worth reading as data (rain over a month, temperature against last year): `chart`.
Indoor climate or a thermostat: `control` or `status`.
Several places compared on one number: `table`.

types.summary: How to get from A to B: total time and arrival, the legs as a bar and as steps, live delays, when to leave, and Open in Maps.
limits: 1–12 legs; ≤ 3 alerts; ≤ 500 path points.
Labels ≤ 80 characters; line names ≤ 16.
`map` needs lat and lon on `from` and `to` (in the schema).
Distances in metres, durations in seconds: the client formats them.
types.fallback: The destination, when to leave, the total time and arrival, the live status, then the legs in one line each and the Maps link. Example: “To the dentist: leave home at 10:16 AM, 24 min, arrive 10:40 AM. On time (MTA live, 10:12 AM). Walk 0.2 mi to Union Sq station (4 min); Q train toward 96 St at 10:20, 3 stops; walk 0.4 mi to 200 W 57th St (8 min). Maps: https://maps.apple.com/?…”
use: Leaving for an appointment from the agenda: “Leave at 10:16 for the dentist; the Q train is on time.”
Local logistics: a school pickup, a viewing across town, the airport run with a delay.
A drive with a map snapshot and the distance.
A walking or cycling route for a run or a commute.
avoid: Turn-by-turn navigation: Open in Maps (an `open` action).
A multi-stop day or an itinerary: `timeline`, with a `route` for the next leg only.
A place on its own (address, opening hours, Directions): `entity` (place).
A delivery’s progress: `timeline` or `steps`.

types.summary: A boarding pass, ticket, membership card or coupon: big glanceable fields, a scannable code drawn on the device, live status, and Add to Wallet when the producer has a .pkpass.
limits: 1–8 fields; labels ≤ 16 characters, values ≤ 24. A boarding pass needs `trip`.
One code per pass; value ≤ 2,000 characters.
`pkpass` is a hermes-file: path ending in .pkpass; remote passes aren’t fetched.
No secrets beyond what the pass shows: no passport numbers, PINs, full card numbers or account passwords in any field.
types.fallback: The pass in one or two lines with every field and the status, never the code’s value: `<title>, <status>: <from> <time> → <to> <time>. Gate …, seat …, boarding …, group …. <holder>, booking <ref>.` Example: “UA 1187 · United, on time: Newark (EWR) 10:55 AM → San Francisco (SFO) 2:20 PM. Gate C112, seat 14A, boarding 10:25 AM, group 2. Alex Rivera, booking QX7P2L. The pass is in the Hermes app and Wallet.”
use: A boarding pass on the day of the flight, updated when the gate changes.
Event or train tickets, with a barcode and the number of admissions.
A gym membership or library card with the member number as a code.
A coupon or voucher with its code, until it expires (`expires_at`).
avoid: The booking or itinerary itself (times, confirmation, baggage): `details` or `timeline`.
Buying a ticket or changing a seat: `approval`.
The time to boarding as a countdown: `metric` (format countdown).
A door code, a one-time password or any other secret: never in a payload; the app’s secure request handles secrets.

types.cue: health of one thing or many
types.summary: The health of one thing or many: one item renders as a hero with its numbers and the one thing to fix, many as a matrix with problems first.
limits: 1–24 items; the matrix shows 8, then Show all. Names ≤ 60 characters; details ≤ 120; `fix` ≤ 160.
≤ 4 metrics per item, labels ≤ 16 characters.
`layout: compact` takes exactly one item; ≤ 2 row actions per item; one primary action per widget.
types.fallback: Hero: `<name>: <headline>. <detail> (<metrics>). One thing to fix: <fix>.` Matrix: the count, then problems first, one sentence each, then the healthy ones in one sentence. Example: “Homelab: 3 of 6 healthy, 1 down. Cron is down: 2 jobs failed (03:00 and 06:00). Worker needs attention: queue at 1.2k. Backups not checked: last report Tuesday 03:00. API, Web and Postgres are healthy.”
use: A machine’s status: the state in words, CPU, memory, disk, uptime, and the one thing to fix.
System health for many services or scheduled jobs: failures first, each with one line.
A deploy or a device after a change: one healthy line (`layout: compact`).
Smart-home or backup checks, where some items can only be “not checked” or claimed by another system.
avoid: Progress through stages (a CI run, a setup, an order): use `steps`.
Something that must not be missed, with a timeline and a next step: use `alert`.
A single number with a target: use `meter`; numbers with deltas: use `metric`.
Everything is fine and nobody asked: one sentence (“All six services are up.”), no widget. A compact status only after a change the person cares about.

types.summary: Progress through ordered stages — waiting, running (with its own progress), done, failed, skipped, blocked, unknown — with durations and a result line.
limits: 1–20 steps (pipeline 2–6, titles ≤ 16 characters, or the client draws it vertical). Titles ≤ 80; details ≤ 120.
`progress` only on the running step, 0–1. One running step at a time.
Result text ≤ 120, detail ≤ 200. ≤ 2 row actions per step.
types.fallback: Title and where it stands, then the steps in order with their state and duration, then the result. Example: “CI for hermes-app on main (a1f9c2e) failed. Build passed in 48 s; Test failed after 2 min 10 s: 2 tests failed in SnapshotTests (testDarkContrastPaywall, testListEmpty); Deploy was skipped.”
use: Multi-step agent progress: “Setting up Trailhead, step 3 of 5”, updated as each stage finishes.

A CI or release run (`kind: pipeline`): Build, Test, Deploy, with the failed stage marked. The `gh-run` parser fills it from `gh run view --json …,jobs`; `junit` fills one step per suite (failed first) and the result line.
Order stages: ordered, shipped, customs, out for delivery, delivered, with the stage that needs the person marked blocked.
A long task inside a stack or a report: `kind: compact`.
avoid: A fully passing run nobody is waiting on: one sentence (“CI passed on main in 3 min.”), no widget.
Steps the person follows themselves (a recipe, a setup they do): use `guide`.
Things to tick off in any order: use `checklist`. Dated events that already happened: use `timeline`.
The health of things rather than progress: use `status`; a failure that must not be missed, with impact and a next step: use `alert`.

types.cue: must not be missed; an incident
types.summary: Something that must not be missed — a failed payment, an outage, a change that affects the person — as a tinted card with what happened and what to do first.
limits: Headline ≤ 200 characters; next ≤ 140; impact ≤ 40.
Timeline ≤ 5 lines of ≤ 100 characters.
One alert per reply; ≤ 2 buttons on the row.
types.fallback: Severity and status first, then the headline, the facts, the timeline and the next step: “Critical, ongoing: Trailhead checkout is down. Orders since 2:02 PM are failing; impact: all checkouts; status: investigating. 2:02 PM 5xx on /api/checkout; 2:06 PM ops paged; 2:15 PM Stripe reports a partial outage. Next: switch checkout to the backup provider (needs your OK).”
use: A payment failed and a service will stop: what, until when, and the next step.
An incident: checkout down, a server unreachable, backups failing for days, with impact, status and a short timeline.
A change the person would otherwise be surprised by (info): clocks going back, a routine moved, an account about to expire.
avoid: Routine news, a daily report or anything promotional: use `summary` or prose. Never marketing.
The health of things that are fine or merely watched: use `status`.
A failed run with its stages: use `steps` (with the result line).
Asking permission to act: use `approval`; a question: use `choice`. More than one alert in a reply: lead with the worst, put the rest in a `status`.

types.summary: One question with set answers — a list, buttons, chips, a rating, times to pick, or several to tick — answered with one tap; plus suggested follow-ups the person can send as their own words.
limits: Options: buttons 2–3, list and chips ≤ 8, times ≤ 12 slots over ≤ 4 days, rating 5 (stars, scale) or 2 (thumbs), suggestions ≤ 3.
Labels ≤ 24 for buttons and chips, ≤ 80 otherwise; suggestion labels ≤ 80 and written as the person would say them. Details ≤ 120; the question ≤ 160.
At most one `recommended`. `select: many` only with list or chips; `preselected` only with many.
types.fallback: The question, then the options numbered with their details (the recommended one marked), then how to answer in words. Example: “Which flight should I book for Tuesday? 1) UA 1187, 10:55 AM → 2:20 PM, nonstop, $286 (recommended). 2) DL 1213, 7:00 AM → 12:35 PM via Atlanta, $242. 3) B6 915, 1:20 PM → 4:45 PM, nonstop, $321. Reply with the flight.” Suggestions: “You could ask next: “…”, “…” or “…”.”
use: Pick one of a few options found for you: flights, flats to view, a restaurant, with the recommended one marked.
Pick a time from slots someone offered (`style: times`), with “None of these work”.
Tick several (`select: many`): which apps a weekly report covers; a plan to approve step by step, with every step preselected.
Quick feedback (`style: rating`); a yes / no / later question (`buttons` or `chips`).
Up to three follow-ups after a reply when the next step is genuinely open (`style: suggestions`).
avoid: Anything that buys, sends, publishes, deletes or spends: use `approval`. Choosing a flight is a `choice`; buying it is an `approval` after.
More than one question, or answers the person must type: use `form`.
Options that need side-by-side criteria and scores: use `compare` (its `answer` picks one).
An open question with no set answers: ask it in prose. Suggestions as a menu of everything the agent can do: no; at most three real next steps.

types.summary: A few things the agent needs filled in — text, numbers, dates, times, a menu, a switch — prefilled where it can, sent in one go.
limits: 1–5 fields; labels ≤ 40 characters; placeholders ≤ 60; help ≤ 120.
Choice fields 2–12 options. Text ≤ 200 characters by default, long text ≤ 2,000.
No password, PIN, key or card-number fields: the plugin rejects labels that ask for secrets.
types.fallback: What the agent needs, one item per field with the prefilled value as a question, then how to answer: “To search for a lake house in Tahoe I need: who’s coming (4 adults, 2 kids?), arrival date (Fri, Oct 30?), budget per night ($250–350?), and anything else that matters. Reply with your answers.” Sent: the values as one sentence and the resolution.
use: A clarification before a search: who’s coming, dates, a budget.
Checking what the agent read from a photo or an email before it files it: an expense from a receipt, an appointment from a letter.
A short request the agent will act on: a lunch preference, a meeting length and time.
A setup detail for a scheduled task: what time, how often, where to send it.
avoid: One question with set answers: use `choice`.
Passwords, API keys, card numbers or any secret: never in a form; Hermes asks with its own secure request.
Anything that buys, sends or spends: the form gathers details, then the agent sends an `approval`.
More than five fields or a long questionnaire: ask the most important things first, or ask in prose.

types.summary: The agent asks permission for a real-world action — send, buy, publish, delete, spend, book — with every consequence spelled out and the answers as tiles.
limits: One subject per approval; ≤ 12 line items; message text ≤ 4,000 characters.
`expires_at` is required for purchase, spend and booking (the client rejects an open-ended money approval).
`consequences.affects` and `consequences.reversible` are required; `cost` is required whenever money moves.
types.fallback: Starts with the question, then every consequence and how to answer: “Lunch order, needs your OK: Green Bowl, chicken bowl and lemonade, $14.50, delivered at 12:30 PM. Paying can’t be undone after 11:40 AM. This request expires at 11:30 AM. Reply “approve”, “edit” or “reject”.” The agent must accept those words as answers on platforms without widgets.
use: Buying: a lunch order, a ticket, a renewal.
Sending a message or email for the person (a draft).
Publishing: a post, a release, a reply to a review.
Spending: an ad budget, a top-up. Deleting: files, backups, accounts.
avoid: Commands Hermes wants to run on the computer: those use the app’s own command approval (it docks above the composer), not a widget.
A plain question with no real-world effect: use `choice`.
Confirming something already done: use `receipt`.
Several unrelated actions: one approval per action.

types.cue: proof of what was done, with undo
types.summary: Proof that something was done: what, the key facts, the confirmation, and Undo while it’s still possible.
limits: Headline ≤ 60 characters, detail ≤ 120. 1–6 facts (labels ≤ 40, details ≤ 60).
At most one Undo, and none once `undone` is set (checked by the schema). `confirmation` is required and not a claim.
Masked payment and account details only (“Visa •• 4242”); never a full number, a password or a key. Money receipts are `sensitivity: private`.
types.fallback: The headline, the facts in one sentence, then the undo line with the word to reply: “Lunch ordered from Green Bowl: $14.50 paid with Visa •• 4242, order #GB-2291, arriving at the office at 12:30 PM. You can cancel until 11:40 AM: reply “undo”.” After an undo: “Order cancelled: $14.50 refunded to Visa •• 4242 in 3–5 days.”
use: After an approval was carried out: “Lunch ordered”, “Table booked”, “Message sent to Mom” (set `in_reply_to` to the approval’s id).
Something with a reference to keep: an order or booking number, a ticket, an invoice paid.
Anything the provider lets you take back for a while: a scheduled post, an order before the kitchen starts, a calendar invite before it’s seen.
The result of an undo: the same widget updated (`rev` + 1) with `undone`.
avoid: Asking before acting: use `approval`. A receipt is only for what already happened.
An action that is still in progress or unconfirmed (“Order sent, waiting for the restaurant”): use `steps` with the step pending, or say it in prose.
Routine actions with nothing to keep or undo (“Added milk to the list”): one sentence, no widget.
Long specs or booking details with many fields: use `details`; a travel booking with a boarding pass uses `pass`.
Commands Hermes ran on the computer: the transcript’s own tool steps show them, not a receipt.

types.summary: Live controls for one smart-home device: switch, slider, stepper, scenes or modes, where every change is a request shown pending until the device reports back.
limits: One device or group per widget; 1–4 controls; scenes 2–8 options, segmented 2–4.

Per kind (checked by the schema): switch takes a boolean and nothing else; slider and stepper need `min` and `max` and take a number; scenes and segmented need `options` and take an option id. Every value may be null (unknown).
Labels ≤ 40 characters; device status ≤ 60.
No `lock` or `alarm` kinds exist: security devices are always an `approval`.
types.fallback: The device, its state and each control’s value in one sentence, then what the person can ask: “Ceiling lights in the living room: on, brightness 60%, scene Relax. Tell me to change the brightness or the scene, or to turn them off.” Unknown values are said as unknown (“brightness unknown: the bridge isn’t answering”).
use: Lights in a room: power, brightness and scenes (“Relax”, “Movie”).
A thermostat: target temperature with the current reading, and modes (Heat, Eco, Off).
A plug, a fan, blinds, a speaker’s volume: one switch or slider with the device’s status.
avoid: Locks, alarms, garage doors, gates, cameras or anything that lets people in or turns protection off: never as a control. Each change is an `approval` (verb Unlock, Disarm; authentication required).
Reading a device without changing it (energy use, temperature over a week): use `metric` or `chart`.
Changing many devices at once or on a schedule (“turn everything off at 23:00”): use `choice` to confirm, then a `receipt`; a recurring routine is a Task.
Anything that spends or orders (a top-up, a filter delivery): use `approval`.

types.cue: TL;DR with a do-first; news; standup
types.summary: The TL;DR: one line that matters, up to five points with a state dot, and the one thing to do first; or a news story with why it matters; or a team standup.
limits: TL;DR ≤ 160 characters (required for brief). 0–5 points, each ≤ 160, emphasis ≤ 60 and a prefix of the text. One do first.
Story: headline ≤ 120, body and why ≤ 280, 1–8 sources.
Standup: 1–8 members; each line ≤ 160.
types.fallback: Brief: the TL;DR, then one line per point, then “Do first: …”. Example: “A light day: two meetings, rain after 4, and the passport renewal is now 3 days late. Dentist at 11 AM, leave at 10:40. Sales up 12% yesterday, $1,284 so far today. 3 support tickets waiting, 1 urgent. Rain from 4 PM. Do first: renew the passport; the form is filled in.” Story: “[Rumor] <headline> (<who reports it>). Why it matters: …” Standup: “Ops: done rolled back checkout; today post-mortem; blocked on Stripe’s report.”
use: A morning brief or the top of a scheduled report: “A light day: two meetings, rain after 4, and the passport renewal is now 3 days late.”
A news story or a daily news brief item, tagged confirmed or rumour, with why it matters for the person’s apps, money or plans.
A team or Bot standup: done, today, blocked, per member.
Appointment preparation (calm, `sensitivity: private`): the TL;DR (“Dr Patel at 10:30 tomorrow”), points led by “Ask:” and “Bring:”, do first “Leave at 10:05”.
avoid: A list to work through or tick off: use `list` or `checklist`. Points are what matters, not everything.
Numbers worth reading as numbers: use `metric` (a summary point can mention one).
Several news stories with links to read: use `sources` or a `stack` of stories; a research verdict with criteria uses `verdict`.
A quiet day with nothing to say: one sentence, or the empty state in a scheduled report. Everything fine deserves one line, not a widget.
Status of systems or jobs: use `status`.

types.summary: Steps the person follows at their own pace, with what they’ll need first, a timer on the steps that have one, and Back / Next on the device.
limits: 2–20 steps; titles ≤ 160 characters, bodies ≤ 1,200, check and caution ≤ 120.
Up to 30 needs; one image per step.
Timers are seconds on the device; a reply carries only the step id.
types.fallback: The title and serving line, the needs as a list with amounts, then the numbered steps with timers in brackets: “Chicken satay bowl (25 min, serves 2). You’ll need: 14 oz chicken thighs, ¾ cup rice, 4 tbsp satay sauce, 1 cucumber… 1. Cook the rice in 1.5× its volume of water. 2. Simmer the chicken in the satay sauce until it thickens (12 min). 3. Slice the cucumber and carrot thinly.”
use: A recipe: ingredients with amounts (scaled locally when `servings` is given), steps with timers.
Setup instructions: pairing a bridge, moving a router, installing a printer driver, with a photo where a part is hard to find.
An exercise routine or rehab session: one movement per step with a hold timer and a caution line (`layout: compact` fits a phone on the floor).
avoid: Work the agent is doing (a deploy, a migration): use `steps`; a guide is for the person to follow.
Things to tick off in any order (packing, a shopping list): use `checklist`.
One or two instructions: write them in the prose.
A schedule of sessions over a week: use `agenda`.

types.summary: Two to four options side by side on the same criteria, the recommended one outlined in ink, and what decided it in one sentence; the weights can be the person’s own.
limits: 2–4 options; 1–8 criteria; ≤ 4 pros and ≤ 4 cons per option, ≤ 60 characters each.
Weights are integers 0–5; scores integers 1–5.
Names ≤ 40 characters, values as text ≤ 40, `decided_by` ≤ 160.
One image per option; images only when every option has one (grid).
types.fallback: The question, then one line per option with its values in criterion order, then the pick and why: “Headphones for travel (under $600): Sony XM6 $399, battery 40 h, noise cancelling best, 8.8 oz. Bose QC Ultra $429, 24 h, best, 9 oz. AirPods Max 2 $549, 20 h, very good, 13.6 oz. Pick: Sony XM6, the same noise cancelling for less, with twice the battery.” With `choose`, end with how to answer in words: “Reply with the one you want.”
use: Buying one of a few products: headphones under $600, a stroller, a laptop.
Choosing a service or approach: where to host the push relay, which CI runner, Postgres or SQLite for an app.
Two or three flats or flights when the person must trade price against commute or time.
A personal decision where the weights are the person’s: set `adjustable` and `choose`.
avoid: One option, or one thing described in detail: use `entity`.
A decision with a confidence and criteria that pass or fail (is this safe, is this ready): use `verdict`.
More than four options, or many attributes per item: use `table` (with `sortable`).
Sides with scores in a match, a poll or an A/B test: use `scoreboard`.
A plain question with set answers and no data to weigh: use `choice`.

types.summary: Who handed what to whom and how it’s going: one Bot asks another (or a person) to do part of the work, and the result comes back here.
limits: One handoff per card; task title ≤ 80 characters, brief ≤ 400.
Activity ≤ 80 characters; result summary ≤ 120; decline reason ≤ 160.
`chat` only for a Bot on the same gateway.
types.fallback: Who asked whom for what, the brief, then where it stands: “Hermes asked Ada to draft the 1.3 release notes: “Draft release notes from the 23 merged PRs, grouped like last time. Check with the user before publishing.” Ada is writing (2 of 4 sections).” When done: “Ada finished the 1.3 release notes (412 words, 3 sections): release-notes-1.3.md.” When declined, the reason.
use: Hermes hands a task to one of the person’s Bots and wants to show it’s in hand: “Hermes asked Ada to draft the 1.3 release notes”.
A Bot passes something to another Bot that owns it: Scout sends a flat to the Bot that books viewings.
The result of a handoff came back: “Ada finished · Release notes for 1.3”, with Read the Draft.
A Bot declined (no access, out of scope) and the person should know who has it now.
avoid: Helpers (sub-agents) inside one turn: those are the app’s team card (`Subagents.teamCard`), not a widget.
A multi-step job one agent runs itself: use `steps`.
Asking the person to do something: use `choice`, `form` or `checklist` (a handoff to a person is for work they take away, not a question).
A finished job with nothing to open: write one sentence, or use `receipt` if it can be undone.

types.summary: A review session of flashcards: the question, revealed on tap on the device, then how well you knew it; the ratings go to the agent in one message at the end, and it schedules the next review.
limits: 0–20 cards per payload; a longer session comes in batches (`progress.total`), one `rate` per batch.
Front and back ≤ 200 characters; example ≤ 200; hint ≤ 120; interval labels ≤ 12.
One media per card.
types.fallback: The deck, the progress, then the first card’s question and how to answer in words: “Spanish · shopping, 6 cards (6 due today). Card 1: How do you say “receipt”? Reply with the answer, then again, hard, good or easy.” Never include the back: without widgets the person answers in words and the agent checks the answer, and a preview must not give it away.
use: Daily review of a deck the agent keeps: “Spanish · shopping, 12 due today”.
Cards Hermes made from something the person read or saved: a chapter, a talk, an article.
Image cards: road signs for a driving test, bones, plants, kanji.
Quick self-tests before an exam or an interview.

A deck in a file: `from_file` with `parser: csv` or `tsv` (an Anki or spreadsheet export; columns `front`, `back`, optional `example` and `hint`) fills `cards`; `json` with a `map` works for the agent’s own deck file. The agent still sets `intervals` from its scheduler.
avoid: A quiz question with set answers where one is right: use `choice`.
Steps to follow: use `guide`.
Reading material or a summary to remember: use `summary` (or `outline`).
A list of words with translations to look at, not test: use `table` or `list`.

types.cue: a scheduled report of several widgets
types.summary: Several widgets sent as one: a scheduled report or brief with a header line (who and when), its widgets in order, in sections that fold, as rows, a carousel or a grid.
limits: 2–8 children; never a stack inside a stack. A stack counts as one of the three directives per reply.
≤ 4 sections; section labels ≤ 40 characters; tag ≤ 16.
The whole payload, children included, ≤ 64 KB; the stack’s `fallback_text` ≤ 4,000 characters, each child’s ≤ 2,000.
Carousel: 2–8 children of one type.
types.fallback: The header line, then each child’s `fallback_text` in order, one paragraph each, a section’s label leading its first paragraph (“Today: …”): “Morning brief (Hermes, daily at 7 AM, Friday, Oct 16). A light day: … Today: 9–9:30 AM Stand-up … Needs doing: Overdue: renew the passport … Yesterday: installs 1,204 (+12%) …”. The stack’s `fallback_text` may run to 4,000 characters (each child’s own stays ≤ 2,000), so every child’s text fits whole.
use: A scheduled brief: “Morning brief · Daily at 7 AM”: summary with the one thing to do first, the agenda, overdue tasks, yesterday’s numbers.
A report that should open folded: the evening homelab report (`layout: collapsed`), problems first, each row unfolding in place.
Several things of one type to swipe through: tonight’s new flats, three meal options (`layout: carousel` of `entity`).
A dashboard-like weekly report on iPad and Mac: revenue, budget, installs, keyword movers (`layout: grid`).
avoid: A normal reply: send one to three separate widgets, each after its sentence.
Many items of one kind in rows: use `list` (or `table`); a stack of eight `entity` cards is a list with images.
Steps of one job: use `steps`; a digest of changes: use `list` with groups and summary counts.
A report with nothing to say (“all quiet”): one sentence, no stack.
Another stack inside a stack: never; flatten it.
